web_evidence.title: Fulfilling the Search for Completeness in Harper Lee’s To Kill A Mockingbird and Delia Owens’ Where the Crawdads Sing
web_evidence.note: A Seton Hall University MA thesis identifies Mockingbird as Scout's first-person narrative, structured as an adult's linear retrospective of events she witnessed in childhood.

web_evidence.title: Reliably Unreliable: An Analysis of the Child Narrators in To Kill a Mockingbird (1960) and Room (2010)
web_evidence.note: This University of Barcelona narratological study analyzes Scout as the novel's retrospective narrating I and distinguishes the adult narrator from the experiencing child.

web_evidence.title: To Kill a Mockingbird: Point of View
web_evidence.note: The opened point-of-view analysis explicitly says the novel is first person, Scout is narrator and protagonist, and she remains narrator throughout the book even when she becomes an observer during the trial.

web_evidence.title: To Kill a Mockingbird | National Endowment for the Arts
web_evidence.note: The NEA Big Read guide describes Scout's perspective and refers to the adult Scout beginning and developing her own narrative, corroborating her role as participating retrospective narrator.

search_log: Searched "To Kill a Mockingbird Harper Lee official publisher excerpt first chapter Scout narrator" and related publisher, author, library, and Google Books excerpt queries.

Opened the Google Books HarperCollins edition page; it supplied publisher metadata and a limited-preview listing but no usable sustained prose in the accessible page, so it was not treated as person evidence.
Searched "To Kill a Mockingbird point of view Scout narrator scholarly analysis" and opened relevant university-repository results from Seton Hall and the University of Barcelona.
Opened the National Endowment for the Arts Big Read guide and SparkNotes point-of-view analysis to verify Scout's role and whole-book scope.

Searched targeted combinations for "alternating narrators," "frame narrative," "epistolary," and "multiple narrators"; results consistently described Scout as the continuing first-person narrator and produced no evidence of sustained base narration in another person.
person_note: The controlling narrator is Jean Louise "Scout" Finch, a participant retrospectively recounting her childhood in first person. Event passages independently expose her narratorial I, me, we, and our, while most other first- or second-person forms in the quote set belong to local dialogue or maxims. q01059 appears to be Scout's base narration despite its upstream dialogue bucket. Two scholarly structural analyses and additional credible whole-book descriptions agree that Scout narrates the novel in first person, with no sustained third- or second-person base sections. The only material uncertainty concerns isolated quote bucketing, not the book-level narrative structure.
